debate.situation: You are the one who always initiates plans with a friend. Time together is lovely, but when you stop texting, contact stops. What is known: the pattern, and that the meetings feel good. What is unknown: why your friend does not initiate (busy, shy, takes you to be happy leading, or less invested) and how much the imbalance bothers you versus how much you want the friendship.

minds.title: The Friendship Philosopher
minds.concern: Whether the friendship has real mutual goodwill, and what kind of friendship it is.
minds.author: Aristotle

minds.title: The Boundary Coach
minds.concern: Saying what you need plainly, without blame, and without over-functioning for the relationship.
minds.author: Harriet Lerner

minds.title: The Skeptical Statistician
minds.concern: Not mistaking a story for evidence: what one pattern of texts does and does not show.
minds.author: Daniel Kahneman

debate.speaker: The Boundary Coach
debate.text: Say something. You are doing all the work of keeping this alive, and quiet resentment is worse than an awkward sentence. A friendly, specific remark, like noticing that you are always the one to reach out, gives your friend a chance to step up.
debate.author: Harriet Lerner
debate.basis: Basis: Harriet Lerner, The Dance of Anger

debate.speaker: The Skeptical Statistician
debate.text: Slow down. You have one pattern and a dozen possible causes. Maybe your friend is overwhelmed, or assumes you like organizing. We tend to build a tidy story from whatever evidence is in front of us and ignore what is missing. What do you actually know?
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Friendship Philosopher
debate.text: But the pattern is not nothing. Aristotle held that friends wish each other well and that this goodwill must be returned and recognised. Delightful evenings can come from a friendship of pleasure, and those fade when the effort dries up. Silence from one side tells you something about what kind this is.
debate.author: Aristotle

debate.speaker: The Skeptical Statistician
debate.text: Tells you something, yes, but less than you think. Warm meetings are also data. Someone who enjoys you and does not initiate fits several stories, including shyness. Before judging the kind of friendship, test it cheaply, because a confrontation based on a guess may land as an accusation.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Boundary Coach
debate.text: I partly agree, but a test can be a way of avoiding the sentence. If you quietly stop texting to see what happens, you have set a trap and will read the silence however it hurts most. I would rather you speak lightly and honestly than run an experiment on your friend.
debate.author: Harriet Lerner
debate.basis: Basis: Harriet Lerner, The Dance of Anger

debate.speaker: The Friendship Philosopher
debate.text: The Coach has a point, and I would add that Aristotle valued friends spending their lives together, which needs shared effort over time. But I go further than Aristotle here: a gentle word is itself an act of goodwill, because it treats your friend as someone able to respond.
debate.author: Aristotle

debate.speaker: The Skeptical Statistician
debate.text: Fine, speaking is not a trap. But the wording matters. Saying you never reach out is an accusation built on a story. Saying you have noticed you usually make the plans, and asking how that looks from their side, invites information instead of defence. That version I can accept.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Boundary Coach
debate.text: Good, and I would add a limit. Raising it is not a promise they will change. If you say it kindly and nothing shifts, your question becomes how much you want to carry. That is your decision about your own effort, not a punishment for them.
debate.author: Harriet Lerner
debate.basis: Basis: Harriet Lerner, The Dance of Anger

debate.speaker: The Friendship Philosopher
debate.text: And here I disagree with doing less by default. Some friendships are worth carrying more of, if you value the person and the evenings are good. Not every imbalance is an injury. Perhaps the question is whether you mind the imbalance, or whether you mind not knowing you are wanted.
debate.author: Aristotle

debate.speaker: The Skeptical Statistician
debate.text: That is a distinction worth keeping, and the answer decides a lot. If it is the effort, a conversation about sharing it fits. If it is the doubt, one warm question may settle more than months of counting texts. I would not guess which one it is for you.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.clearer: The main insight is that there are two separate questions hiding in one: whether your friend values you, and whether you are willing to keep carrying the planning. A light, curious remark was the least risky way to learn more, but the minds disagreed about whether to test with silence first and about whether an imbalance is a problem at all. A possible reflection: does the imbalance itself bother you, or the uncertainty about whether you are wanted?
debate.dependsOn: If the planning effort is what wears on you, then raising it kindly makes sense, because it invites your friend to share the load and tells you whether they will. If your real worry is whether the friend cares, then a warm, direct question about how they see the friendship fits better, because it addresses the doubt without assuming an answer. If you enjoy the friendship and do not mind being the organiser, then saying nothing, or simply continuing, is reasonable, because the imbalance may be a fact about roles rather than a problem. If you do not know why your friend does not initiate, the proportionate way to learn is a single easygoing conversation, or a modest pause in your own planning after you have said something, not a long silence kept as a secret test.
